records.name: Rio de Jeneiro
records.current_summary:
Rio de Janeiro recorded only 3 trans killings in 2025 (a low rate of ~0.18/million against a population of ~17 M), well below the national average. However, two distinct visitor-facing signals pull the score modestly below the national 0.71: a documented extortion pattern in Niterói and a tourist-targeting scam in Copacabana.

In January–February 2026, multiple trans sex workers in central Niterói reported a two-year coercive regime: a man claiming militia and public-agent connections forced them to pay R$120 per week each and had 'almost strangled three of the girls.' The alleged extorter was an ex-employee of Niterói city hall, arrested in 'Operação Ronda Sumbria' by the 76ª DP, and remanded in pre-trial custody. The institutional response was mixed—arrests and dismissal occurred, but the racket operated under the appearance of state backing for roughly two years before intervention. Trans council member Benny Briolly brought the case to the Public Ministry.

Separately, in Copacabana the tourist police (Deat) arrested two trans women caught extorting a Norwegian tourist with threats to circulate intimate videos—a documented, visitor-facing scam vector. The killing rate is low, but the coercive pattern with state implication and the tourist-targeting scam justify a deviation of about 0.03 below national. Compared with São Paulo (no deviation), Rio's risk is qualitative rather than numerical.

sources.claim: Extra/Rio (updated 12 Feb 2026): the Rio de Janeiro state court (TJ-RJ) decreed preventive detention of a man accused of exploiting trans women in Niteroi; the suspect was a city-hall employee there until January 2026. Pre-trial custody confirmed in the extortion case this record documents.

Tupi FM (3 Apr 2025): Rio's tourism police (DEAT) arrested two trans women in flagrante for extorting a Norwegian tourist in Copacabana, Zona Sul. Visitor-directed extortion arrests on the beach strip — the tourist-targeting scam signal this record scores.

National dossier — the table behind this record's 2025 state count. Supports this record's 3-killings figure (~0.18/million, below national).

records.name: Goias
records.current_summary:
Goiás recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, placing it in the national mid-band alongside Maranhão and Pará. Against a population of ~7.2 million the rate is about 0.69 per million per year, roughly 1.8× the national rate (80 killings across ~211 million). Goiás sits on the Cerrado agricultural frontier, and the ANTRA dossier finds 67.5% of Brazilian trans killings occur in interior cities outside the capitals - where monitoring, reporting and access to public policy are weaker - so a visitor away from the capital shares this interior exposure.

No Goiás-specific ordinance, legal restriction or protection measure was identified in the dossier; the state's risk profile rests on the above-national per-capita killing count and the interior-concentration pattern. The companion 2024 national dossier (122 killings, 16% below 2023) recorded the same ~68% outside-capitals share.

National dossier — the table behind this record's 2025 state count. Supplies this record's 2025 count (5 of 80).

Sergipe Em Debate (27 Jan 2025): ANTRA's previous-year dossier recorded 122 trans and travesti killings in Brazil in 2024, 16% below 2023, five of the victims rights defenders. Companion dossier this record cites for its 2024 comparison year.

records.name: Maranhao
records.current_summary:
Maranhão recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — the same count the association dossier logged for it in 2024 — so its position in the ranking's middle-upper band is persistent rather than a one-year spike (SBT News, 26 January 2026; CNN Brasil, 27 January 2025). No Maranhão-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement policy affecting trans people is documented in the audited sources; federal law applies uniformly.

The national profile the dossiers attach to this state's region — victims young, Black, poor and Northeastern; 97% travestis and trans women; most killings in public places, at night, and outside state capitals where monitoring and policy access are thinner — maps onto Maranhão's place in both tables. The documented risk is structural exposure: two consecutive years of above-median lethal counts in a country that leads the world's tallies, without any local legal change either way.

records.name: Para
records.current_summary:
Pará recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, in the middle band of the ANTRA dossier's state ranking of that year's 80 national killings (SBT News, 26 January 2026). No Pará-specific statute, ordinance or policy affecting trans people was found in the audited sources; the federal framework applies uniformly. The second audited source lists the 2024 worst-hit states without naming this state, so its 2024 position cannot be fixed from the record.

What the dossiers do document bears directly on a vast Amazonian state: roughly two-thirds to 68% of such killings nationally occur in interior cities outside the capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker, and victims are overwhelmingly young Black travestis and trans women killed in public places. For a trans visitor travelling beyond the main metropolitan area, the least-monitored geography is precisely where the recorded killings sit.

records.name: Alagoas
records.current_summary:
Alagoas recorded 6 killings of trans and travesti people in 2024 — among the elevated small-state totals in that year's ANTRA dossier table (CNN Brasil, 27 January 2025) — and 2 in 2025 (SBT News, 26 January 2026). No Alagoas-specific legal restriction or enforcement finding is documented; federal law applies uniformly.

The swing between consecutive dossiers on a small population is itself the finding: at these denominators a couple of cases moves a state's position sharply, which is why the monitoring body cautions that falling national counts reflect violence shifting into attempted homicides and persistent under-recording (misclassification of victims' gender identity degrades the data) rather than improving safety. The victim profile the dossiers attach to this region — young, Black, poor, Northeastern, killed in public places at night — places risk wherever a visibly trans person is in public, in a state inside the country's hardest-hit region.

records.name: Mato Grosso
records.current_summary:
Mato Grosso recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 on a population of ~3.6 million - about 0.83 per million per year, more than double the national rate, and the 2024 dossier counted 8 killings in the state, its highest year. The state sits on the Cerrado/agribusiness frontier, where the dossier's finding that most killings happen outside the capitals means small-town exposure is relevant for visitors travelling beyond Cuiabá.

Three cases on a small population is statistically fragile, and no qualitative incident, ordinance or enforcement evidence was found beyond the ANTRA counts; the elevated per-capita reading therefore carries a smaller weight than the raw rate suggests.

sources.claim: ANTRA's 9th annual dossier (released 26 Jan 2026, reported by SBT News): Brazil recorded 80 murders of trans and travesti people in 2025, 34% down on 2024 but with at least 75 attempted homicides and crimes marked by excessive violence; per-state 2025 counts - Ceara and Minas Gerais 8 each, Bahia and Pernambuco 7 each, Goias, Maranhao and Para 5 each, Alagoas 2, Mato Grosso 3; 1,261 murders over 2017-2025 (avg 140/year); 97% of victims travestis/trans women, over half aged 18-29, 70% Black among racially-identified cases; 67.5% of killings happened in interior cities rather than capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policies are harder; Brazil has led the global ranking since 2008. Lists Mato Grosso at 3 killings for 2025.

sources.title: MT ocupa o 12º lugar em assassinato de pessoas trans e travesti
sources.claim: Diario de Cuiabá, Jan. 27, 2026: Mato Grosso ranked 12th among Brazilian states for killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, against a national total of 80, and the state has recorded 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people since 2017. For this record: a Mato Grosso-specific reading of the same ANTRA dossier the summary cites for the state's 3 killings in 2025.

sources.title: Empresário é condenado a 13 anos de prisão por morte de mulher trans em MT
sources.claim: G1 MT, Apr. 16, 2026: businessman Jorlan Cristiano Ferreira, 44, was sentenced by a jury to 13 years and 6 months in prison for the feminicide of trans woman Mayla — found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 on a farm beside MT-485 in Sorriso — plus procedural fraud and corpse concealment; the jury held the killing was motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination. For this record: a documented Mato Grosso conviction that explicitly recognizes the gender dimension of a trans woman's killing.

sources.title: Travestis e transexuais têm direito ao uso do nome social em MT
sources.claim: Diario de Cuiabá, Mar. 16, 2021: a decree published in the state's official gazette on Mar. 12, 2021 guarantees travestis and trans people in Mato Grosso the right to use their social name, accepted by state public offices and usable on badges, cards and identification documents, with state employees able to register the social name in internal records and systems and official publications forbidden from using the civil name without consent. For this record: an identified Mato Grosso state-government measure recognizing trans identity, relevant to documents and name usage within the state.

records.name: Comunitat Valenciana
records.current_summary:
The Comunitat Valenciana holds a dedicated integral law on the right to identity and gender expression (Llei de 7 d'abril, integral del reconeixement del dret a la identitat i expressió de gènere) alongside a general LGTBI-protection statute, making it one of only three communities (with Andalucía and Madrid) to have enacted legislation in both the trans-specific and general-LGTBI-equality categories. Unlike Madrid, Valencia has not amended or narrowed its provisions. The statutory framework supports institutional response channels for a visitor encountering discrimination.

No incident data, enforcement action, or negative visitor-facing finding was located for this community in the research pass. Valencia city carries a visible and well-established LGBTQ community with dedicated infrastructure. The divergence from national is modest and rests on the statutory-completeness evidence.

Vs national (0.88): +0.03, reflecting the presence of a dual-category legislative framework (gender identity + LGTBI equality) that is active and unrevised. Vs Madrid (0.83), which shares the dual-category structure but actively rolled back its provisions in 2023, Valencia's position is clearly safer. Vs Castilla y León (0.81), which has no law at all, the gap is 0.10 points driven entirely by the presence versus absence of statutory infrastructure.
records.current_localsOnly: The regional identity-and-expression law's registry and administrative procedures operate for residents; a visitor never invokes them.

sources.claim: Spanish trans-rights platform's inventory of autonomous-community gender-identity laws, listing Comunitat Valenciana with two statutes: Ley 8/2017 of 7 April (integral recognition of the right to gender identity and expression) and Ley 23/2018 of 29 November (LGTBI equality) — the two-statute combination the record's framework claim rests on. Neighbouring communities listed for contrast carry only single statutes (e.g. Cataluña Ley 11/2014, Aragón Ley 4/2018).

LGTBI federation's 2025 radiography of public educational policies across Spanish regions: tracks which autonomidades have gender-identity protocols and education legislation; notes the Valencian parliament completing its gender legislation and groups the Comunidad Valenciana with Madrid, Extremadura, Murcia and Navarra among the leaders on educational policy coverage.

sources.title: BOE-A-2017-5118 Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresión de género en la Comunitat Valenciana. - BOE
sources.claim: Official gazette text of the Comunitat Valenciana's Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresion de genero, published as BOE-A-2017-5118. Article 1 makes the law's purpose the guarantee of an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth, and public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana must treat people according to their felt gender identity; Title III provides for administrative documentation and an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families. Primary legal text confirming the 'dedicated integral law on the right to identity and gender expression' this record cites, enacted 7 April 2017.

sources.title: BOE-A-2019-281 Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI. - BOE
sources.claim: Official gazette text of Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI (BOE-A-2019-281), the Comunitat Valenciana's general equality statute for LGTBI people. Its provisions cover non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, access and admission rights (art. 56), reversal of the burden of proof (art. 57), and a Title V regime of administrative infringements and sanctions (arts. 58-66) for discrimination against LGTBI people. Primary legal text confirming the community's general-LGTBI-statute category alongside its 2017 trans-specific law, the dual-category statutory framework on which this record's assessment rests.

sources.title: Seis meses de carcel por perseguir, insultar y grabar a una persona trans en Valencia - Observatorio de delitos de odio y discriminacion
sources.claim: Report of a conviction by the Audiencia Provincial de Valencia (Section 5) over a June 2022 incident in a Valencia park (Patraix), where an 18-year-old with several minors insulted, chased, recorded and mocked a trans woman solely because of her gender identity. The adult accepted six months' prison, suspended on condition of committing no offence for two years plus payment of a 720-euro fine and 1,000-euro moral-damages indemnity to the victim; two minors had already been sentenced to supervision measures, and the hate-crime prosecutor (fiscal coordinadora de delitos de odio) handled the case. Documents an institutional response channel operating in the community: a gender-identity-motivated offence investigated, charged and resulting in a court sentence in Valencia.

records.name: Buenos Aires
records.current_summary:
Buenos Aires Province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in Argentina: the federal human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police—or by third parties under police cover—against trans and travesti people during operations in La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría, carried out under "preventive policing" frameworks. Academic legal analysis (CELS CEDAW shadow report; UNLP/Pensamiento Penal) confirms that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased use of drug-law prosecution (devolved to provincial justice in 2005) and street-offence law as the operative instrument for indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity—a patterned, state-implicated escalation with impunity.

The deviation from the national score (0.58) is −0.05. No other province has a comparable volume of multi-source, patterned enforcement documentation reaching the UN treaty-body system. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework (drug-law devolution + anti-narcotics security policy) that measurably increased police persecution of trans women. Protective institutions coexist—the provincial defensoría maintains a 2024 registry-rectification guide and documents discrimination caseloads—but these are resident-facing and do not offset the visitor-facing exposure to arbitrary detention during any police stop.

Compared with Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires (0.55), the Province lacks CABA's tribunal contravencional judicial-oversight structure and anti-discrimination apparatus; its police-judge model under the código de faltas gives less post-detention review. Compared with the silent majority of provinces (national score), the difference is one of documented pattern rather than statutory hostility—no BA law criminalises gender identity, but enforcement practice does the work.
records.current_localsOnly: The provincial defensoria's registry-rectification guide and discrimination-caseload machinery serve residents; a visitor never uses them.

sources.claim: Buenos Aires provincial ombudsman's Gender Violence Office (created by Resolución Nº 100/10) submission to the UN Human Rights Committee (June-July 2016 review): documents violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police — or third parties under police cover — against trans and travesti people in Buenos Aires province, in a dedicated section on violence by judicial, state and police agents. This is the record's core 2016 UN-submission claim. Note: 2016-17 UN-review PDFs no longer describe current law — the 2012 federal Gender Identity Law remains in force, but a Dec-2024 national DNU added consent/medical-judicial requirements for minors' gender-affirming care (under litigation).

UNLP thesis documenting the criminalisation of trans and travesti women in Buenos Aires province through drug-offence prosecutions under microtrafficking enforcement, focused on La Plata's Zona Roja — showing that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security-led street-offence policing became the operative indirect-criminalisation instrument in the province. Regional academic evidence for the record's escalation claim.

Pensamiento Penal legal analysis: rising criminalisation of trans/travesti women in Buenos Aires province, particularly La Plata's Zona Roja, and it records that in 2005 Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug-sale and possession offences — the devolution that enabled provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution as the indirect-criminalisation instrument. Supplies the dated 2005 mechanism behind the record's escalation claim.

Provincial Ombudsman's September 2024 guide to gender-marker rectification for people born in Buenos Aires province: registry rectification steps, including provisions for people born in the province now living elsewhere. Dated local procedure evidence — provincial implementation of the 2012 federal Gender Identity Law's recognition regime.
